findings.checklist_item: Correct the premise that docs/mcp-reference.md documents success outputSchemas — it is a generated one-line tool inventory; retarget AC3 to the file that actually documents success schemas (e.g. docs/output-schemas.md) or the generator/source-of-truth, not the generated mcp-reference.md.
evidence: Plan quote: 'docs/mcp-reference.md documents outputSchema for success shapes; the failure shape is undocumented and unpinned'
search_files for 'outputSchema' and 'chema' in docs/mcp-reference.md both return (no matches)
docs/mcp-reference.md:3 'Generated by scripts/gen_mcp_reference.py — do not edit by hand'; the table lists only a Tool | Summary one-liner per tool
Actual outputSchema docs live at docs/output-schemas.md:150-176, docs/api-stability.md:23-25, AGENTS.md:144
findings.finding: The plan asserts 'docs/mcp-reference.md documents outputSchema for success shapes', but that file is a generated tool inventory listing only a one-line description per tool — the string 'outputSchema' (and 'schema') never appears in it. Success outputSchemas are actually documented in docs/output-schemas.md, docs/api-stability.md, and AGENTS.md. AC3 then targets mcp-reference.md as the location to document the failure shape 'alongside the success outputSchemas', a placement that rests on this false premise.
findings.location: Plan section 'Why it matters' and AC3 ('...docs/mcp-reference.md documents it alongside the success outputSchemas')
scenarios: Author edits mcp-reference.md to add the failure shape and the CI drift gate reverts it (file is generated); or the failure shape sits in a doc that never documented success schemas, defeating the 'alongside' intent of AC3.
findings.suggested_fix: Retarget AC3's doc location to docs/output-schemas.md (where success outputSchemas are documented) and/or the generator scripts/gen_mcp_reference.py, rather than the hand-edit-forbidden generated mcp-reference.md.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how the library interface surfaces its error code (e.g. attach the machine code to the raised exception types so library, CLI, and MCP all read the same value) so AC5's three-way cross-interface test is actually constructible.
evidence: _errors.py: RebarError/ConcurrencyError expose returncode/stderr only — no error-code field
_commands/txn.py:50 ConcurrencyMismatch(CommandError) — carries message/returncode, not a machine code
The code (e.g. 'concurrency_conflict') is assigned at the CLI wrapper (claim.py:319), not at the library raise site (txn.py:355)
findings.finding: AC5 requires the library, CLI, and MCP to 'agree on the code for the same failure,' verified by a cross-interface test — but the library interface currently carries no error code. Codes are computed only inside CLI command wrappers; the library raises ConcurrencyMismatch/RebarError/CommandError exceptions exposing returncode/message but no 'error' discriminator. The plan does not say where the library-side code comes from, so a three-way cross-interface test has no library value to compare.
findings.location: AC5 ('the three interfaces (library, CLI, MCP) agree on the code')
findings.suggested_fix: Attach a `error_code` (or equivalent) attribute to the RebarError/ConcurrencyMismatch/CommandError hierarchy at the raise site, and have both the CLI error_envelope call and the MCP surface read it — giving all three interfaces one code to agree on.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile the pre-existing MCP {error, kind} failure shape (_mcp_reads.py explain_criterion) with the new error_envelope — state whether it is migrated, aliased, or exempt — so MCP does not end up with two incompatible failure shapes.
evidence: _mcp_reads.py:66-77: 'On failure returns a structured error {error, kind}' → return {"error": str(exc), "kind": exc.kind}
This shape uses `error` as a human message plus a `kind` discriminator — structurally unlike error_envelope's {error(code), input, message}
findings.finding: The plan asserts MCP 'has no structured error identity at all,' but MCP already returns a divergent partial error shape ({"error": str(exc), "kind": exc.kind}) from explain_criterion. The plan neither acknowledges this existing shape nor says whether it must be migrated to the error_envelope form, risking a second incompatible failure shape on the same interface.
findings.location: 'Only the CLI emits it' / 'The MCP surface has no structured error identity at all'

findings.checklist_item: Specify the fallback error code MCP must emit when a failure maps to no existing CLI code (e.g. a generic 'internal_error'/'unknown_error'), and require it be part of the shared vocabulary and pinned by test.
evidence: ABSENCE: the plan enumerates known CLI codes but gives no rule for MCP-only failure surfaces (e.g. tool-argument validation, transport-level, or engine errors with no existing CLI envelope) — no generic/fallback code is named
T8 checklist item (d): 'a fallback for an incomplete/failed sub-step is specified' — here the failed-sub-step-to-code mapping has an undefined tail
findings.finding: The plan specifies MCP failures 'carry ... at minimum error and message' but never specifies the fallback code for an MCP failure path that maps to no existing CLI code — leaving the agent-consumed discriminator undefined for the residual/unclassified failure case.
findings.location: AC #1 ('at minimum error and message, with input where a target was being resolved')
scenarios: An MCP tool hits a failure with no corresponding CLI code; the implementer either invents an ad-hoc code (recreating interface-only drift) or omits `error`, violating AC #1's 'at minimum error'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State where the error_envelope lives in the MCP response (isError tool-result content, a structured error field, or a declared error variant of the outputSchema) so the delivery contract is unambiguous.
evidence: 'The failure shape is declared in the MCP tool contract so consumers can rely on it'
Body states current failures arrive 'as prose inside an exception message' but never states the target delivery mechanism
MCP has multiple distinct error-return conventions (isError result content vs structured outputSchema); the plan picks none
findings.finding: The plan does not specify HOW the error_envelope is delivered over the MCP transport — whether as an isError tool result, a structured-content error block, a declared error variant of the outputSchema, or a raised exception with structured data. An executor must invent this delivery contract.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria, line 3 ('declared in the MCP tool contract')
scenarios: Executor implements the envelope as a raised exception detail while an agent consumer expects it in the tool-result content, so the discriminator is still unreachable

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile the schema's required `input` field with AC line 1's conditional `input`: either relax the field for target-less failures or specify the sentinel used when no target was being resolved.
evidence: Body: 'input — the raw input that failed to resolve (required)'
AC line 1: 'with input where a target was being resolved' — conditional, not always present
findings.finding: The common.schema.json error_envelope marks `input` as REQUIRED, but AC line 1 makes it conditional ('with input where a target was being resolved'). A target-less MCP failure (e.g. a gate refusal not tied to a ticket) would then either violate the required schema or force a placeholder value. The plan does not reconcile this.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria line 1 vs 'The vocabulary already exists' section
scenarios: A gate refusal with no ticket target emits an envelope with no natural `input`, failing schema validation or requiring a synthetic value

findings.checklist_item: Define WHERE the shared error-code vocabulary lives (e.g. a central enum/registry both the CLI and MCP import) and require it as the single source the cross-interface test asserts against, so AC #2 and AC #5 have a concrete referent.
evidence: common.schema.json:110 — "error": { "type": "string", "description": "Machine error code, e.g. 'ticket_not_found'." } — an example, not an enumerated vocabulary; no `enum` keyword
output.py:132 — `def error_envelope(error: str, ...)` accepts a free string; no code registry
Emitters use inline literals: reads_cli.py:165/170/410 (ticket_not_found/show_failed/deps_failed), claim.py:319 (concurrency_conflict), transition.py:11 (claim_failed) — no shared source

Plan asserts 'give MCP the discriminator the CLI already emits' but the discriminator's VALUE set is implicit, so 'the SAME vocabulary' and 'a code cannot exist on one interface only' have no definable referent
findings.finding: The plan treats the error-code 'vocabulary' as already-defined, but no enum or central registry of codes exists: common.schema.json:110 describes `error` only by example ('e.g. ticket_not_found') with no `enum`, and codes are bare string literals scattered across call sites (ticket_not_found, show_failed, deps_failed, concurrency_conflict, claim_failed, next_batch). AC #2 ('a code cannot exist on one interface only') and AC #5 (cross-interface agreement 'verified by a cross-interface test') both presuppose a single shared vocabulary source the plan neither names nor creates.
findings.location: AC #2 / AC #5; section 'The vocabulary already exists'
scenarios: An implementer emits an MCP code (e.g. 'not_found') that differs in spelling from the CLI's 'ticket_not_found'; without an enum to import, the cross-interface test has nothing canonical to assert against and can silently diverge
A future CLI code is added and MCP is never updated, re-introducing the exact interface-only-code drift the plan aims to prevent
findings.suggested_fix: Add a step introducing a canonical error-code enum/constant set (e.g. in output.py alongside error_envelope) enumerating ticket_not_found, show_failed, deps_failed, concurrency_conflict, claim_failed, etc.; have both CLI emitters and the new MCP emitters draw codes from it; make the cross-interface test iterate that enum so any interface-only or misspelled code fails.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Decide whether error codes get a single shared source of truth (enum/registry) the three interfaces import, or document why a cross-interface test alone durably prevents one-interface-only codes.

AC only mandates a cross-interface TEST, not a shared definition
findings.finding: The plan requires that 'a code cannot exist on one interface only' and that all three interfaces agree, but proposes no single source of truth for the code vocabulary — CLI codes today are string literals scattered across emitters (reads_cli.py:165/170/411, next_batch.py:537, signing.py:786). Enforcing agreement by cross-interface test alone leaves the literals free to drift; a shared registry/enum would make the invariant structural.
scenarios: A new CLI failure code is added as a literal without a corresponding MCP mapping; the test catches it only if the test itself is updated to enumerate it
findings.suggested_fix: Introduce a shared error-code registry (module-level constants or enum) that CLI, library, and MCP all reference, and have the cross-interface test assert against that registry.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Name the single source of truth for the error-code vocabulary (e.g. extract the inline literals into a shared enum/registry that CLI, library, and MCP all reference) so AC2/AC5's 'same vocabulary' and cross-interface test have something to diff against rather than duplicated string literals.
evidence: reads_cli.py:165 error_envelope("ticket_not_found", …); :170 "show_failed"; :410 code = "ticket_not_found" if … else "deps_failed"
claim.py:318 "concurrency_conflict"; :333 "claim_failed" — all inline literals, no shared constant

findings.finding: The CLI 'vocabulary' the plan tells MCP to draw from is not a single source of truth — codes are inline string literals duplicated across emit sites (ticket_not_found, show_failed, deps_failed, concurrency_conflict, claim_failed), with no shared registry/enum. AC2 ('SAME vocabulary… a code cannot exist on one interface only') and AC5 ('cross-interface test, not by inspection') presuppose a shared source to draw from and diff against; without one, the straightforward implementation copies literals into MCP — reproducing exactly the drift the ticket exists to prevent, and leaving nothing for a cross-interface test to key on other than duplicated constants.
findings.location: AC2 / AC5; 'give MCP the discriminator the CLI already emits'
findings.suggested_fix: Add a step to hoist the error codes into one module (e.g. a code constant defined on the raising exception types in _errors.py / _commands/txn.py, or a codes enum), have error_envelope() and the MCP surface both source codes from it, and point the cross-interface test at that single registry.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State a one-line positive rationale for where the error code originates (single shared source vs. per-interface emission) so the implementer builds the drift-resistant approach the ACs demand rather than the easiest one.
evidence: The plan describes WHAT (MCP should emit the envelope) and WHY it matters (agents branch on outcome) but not WHY the emit-site replication approach is preferable to hoisting codes to the exception layer
ABSENCE: no rationale sentence tying the chosen approach to codebase-alignment/blast-radius/testability
findings.finding: The plan states no positive rationale for its chosen approach (replicate the CLI's per-site error_envelope emission into the MCP layer) versus a structurally different alternative such as attaching the machine code to the exception types at the raise site so all three interfaces derive it from one place. Given the drift risk exposed by findings 1-2, the load-bearing design choice (where the code originates) is left implicit.
findings.location: Overall approach ('give MCP the discriminator the CLI already emits')
